tips.title: Two different metals, or nothing happens
tips.body: A simple cell needs **two different metals** in an electrolyte. The same metal twice gives **zero** volts, because there is no difference in reactivity to drive the electrons. The bigger the difference, the bigger the voltage.

tips.title: Flat means a reactant is used up
tips.body: A battery going flat is a **reactant being used up**, never electricity running out. Recharging **reverses the reactions** with an external current; it does not add anything. Both phrasings are marked strictly.

tips.title: Add the halves and watch them cancel
tips.body: **Higher tier.** Two half equations are right only if they **add to the overall reaction** with the **electrons cancelling**. Check atoms and charge in each half first: $2\text{H}_2 \rightarrow 4\text{H}^+ + 4e^-$ has 4 H each side and zero charge each side.

tips.title: Evaluate means decide, and say when
tips.body: For fuel cells against batteries, give points both ways then **commit**, naming the circumstances: a lorry with its own depot, or a family car charged overnight. And remember a fuel cell is only as clean as the **hydrogen supplied to it**.

why.matters:
A displacement reaction hands electrons straight from one metal to the other and all you get is a warm beaker. A **cell** separates the two halves so the electrons have to go the long way round — through a wire, where they can do something useful.

That is the whole idea, and everything portable runs on it. Which metals you pick decides the voltage, whether the reaction can be reversed decides whether it recharges, and feeding the reactants in from outside turns a battery into a fuel cell.

examples.title: Why a flat battery weighs the same as a full one
examples.body:
Nothing has leaked out. A battery goes flat because one of its **reactants has been used up** — the chemicals are still in there, just in their finished form. Electricity was never stored in it; the reaction was.

That is also why some batteries recharge and some do not. Charging pushes the reaction **backwards** with an external current, rebuilding the original chemicals, and it only works if the products will go back. A fuel cell dodges the question entirely by having its reactants delivered from outside.

visual.alt: A table of three power sources: an alkaline battery which stops when a reactant runs out and cannot be restarted, a rechargeable cell whose reaction can be reversed, and a fuel cell which runs as long as fuel is supplied

examples.title: Why two copper coins make no battery at all
examples.body:
The classic lemon battery needs a copper coin **and** a zinc nail. Two coins give nothing, however many lemons you line up, because the voltage comes from the **difference in reactivity** between the two metals — and there is none.

Widen the gap and the voltage grows. Against a copper electrode, iron gives about 0.78 V, zinc about 1.10 V, and magnesium about 2.71 V. The order is the reactivity series, and the numbers are the gap in it.

props.caption: Each paired with copper. The wider the reactivity gap, the more volts.

visual.alt: Three bars in proportion showing the voltage of a simple cell made with copper and each of magnesium, zinc and iron: two point seven one, one point one zero and nought point seven eight volts, in the order of the reactivity series

examples.title: The hydrogen car and the electric one
examples.body:
A hydrogen fuel cell emits only **water** where it is driven, refills in minutes and loses capacity far more slowly than a battery. A rechargeable battery is heavier and slower to fill, but plugs into a socket that already exists.

The honest verdict names the circumstances. A fuel cell is only as clean as the hydrogen, and most hydrogen is currently made from natural gas; there are few places to buy it, and it has to be stored under pressure. For a lorry fleet with its own depot the fuel cell wins. For a family car charged overnight, it does not.

steps.title: What a cell is
steps.body:
A **cell** contains **chemicals which react to produce electricity**. That is the definition, and it is worth having word for word.

The simplest version you need to describe is a **simple cell**: **two different metals in contact with an electrolyte**. Both parts matter.

- **Two different metals.** Two pieces of the same metal produce no voltage at all, because there is nothing to drive electrons one way rather than the other.
- **An electrolyte**, a solution that conducts, completing the circuit between them.

A **battery** is **two or more cells connected together in series**, which gives a **greater voltage** than one cell alone. So strictly a single AA is a cell; four of them in a torch make a battery.

The **voltage produced depends on several factors, including the type of electrode and the electrolyte**. That phrase, *type of electrode and electrolyte*, is what mark schemes look for.

This whole topic is **chemistry only**, not combined science.

steps.title: Rechargeable or not
steps.body:
The difference is about **what happens to the chemicals**, and the specification is precise.

- In **non-rechargeable** cells and batteries, the **chemical reactions stop when one of the reactants has been used up**. **Alkaline batteries are non-rechargeable.**
- **Rechargeable** cells and batteries can be recharged because **the chemical reactions are reversed when an external electrical current is supplied**.

So a rechargeable battery is not refilled with anything. The same chemicals are still inside; supplying a current **runs the reactions backwards**, turning the products back into the reactants.

Two phrasings to avoid.

- "The battery runs out of electricity" earns nothing. It runs out of a **reactant**.
- "Recharging puts more chemicals in" is wrong. Recharging **reverses the reaction**.

steps.title: Fuel cells
steps.body:
A **fuel cell** is different from a battery in one crucial way: it is **supplied by an external source of fuel**, for example **hydrogen**, and **oxygen or air**.

Inside the cell the **fuel is oxidised electrochemically** to **produce a potential difference**. Because the fuel comes from outside, a fuel cell does not go flat while the supply lasts. It is refuelled, not recharged.

In a **hydrogen fuel cell** the **overall reaction is the oxidation of hydrogen to produce water**:

$$2\text{H}_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

That is the same reaction as burning hydrogen, but it happens **electrochemically** rather than as a flame, so the energy comes out as a **potential difference** instead of as heat and light.

The only product is **water**, which is the fuel cell's great selling point and the source of most exam questions about it.

steps.title: Higher tier: the half equations
steps.body:
Writing the **half equations for the electrode reactions** in a hydrogen fuel cell is **Higher tier**.

At the **negative electrode** the hydrogen is **oxidised**, meaning it **loses electrons**:

$$2\text{H}_2 \rightarrow 4\text{H}^+ + 4e^-$$

At the **positive electrode** the oxygen is **reduced**, meaning it **gains electrons**:

$$\text{O}_2 + 4\text{H}^+ + 4e^- \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

Add the two together, and the electrons and the hydrogen ions cancel, leaving the overall reaction $2\text{H}_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. That cancellation is the check that your two halves are right.

A cell with an **alkaline** electrolyte is written differently and is equally acceptable: $2\text{H}_2 + 4\text{OH}^- \rightarrow 4\text{H}_2\text{O} + 4e^-$ at the negative electrode and $\text{O}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + 4e^- \rightarrow 4\text{OH}^-$ at the positive. Those also add to the same overall reaction.

**Oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain.** The electrons appear on the **right** of the oxidation half equation and on the **left** of the reduction one.

steps.title: Your turn: fuel cells against batteries
steps.body:
A car manufacturer is choosing between a **hydrogen fuel cell** and a **rechargeable battery** for a new car.

1. Give **two** advantages of the hydrogen fuel cell.
2. Give **two** disadvantages.
3. State one advantage of the rechargeable battery.
4. Reach a **decision**, and say what it depends on.

Then, for Higher tier practice: write the half equation for the reaction at the **negative** electrode of the fuel cell, and show that it adds with the positive electrode equation to give $2\text{H}_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Part 4 is where the marks separate. An answer that lists points and stops has not evaluated anything.

steps.title: Going deeper: evaluating the fuel cell honestly
steps.body:
The specification asks you to **evaluate the use of hydrogen fuel cells in comparison with rechargeable cells and batteries**. A top answer is even-handed and then decides.

**For the fuel cell.** It produces **only water** at the point of use, so no carbon dioxide and no particulates where people are breathing. It **refuels in minutes** rather than recharging over hours, and it loses capacity far more slowly than a battery does over hundreds of charges. For a given range it is lighter, because you carry fuel rather than a very heavy battery.

**Against the fuel cell.** **Hydrogen is difficult to store**: it must be kept at very high pressure or very low temperature, and it is **explosive**. There are **few refuelling stations**. Fuel cells use **expensive catalysts**. And crucially, the hydrogen has to be **made** — usually from fossil fuels, or by electrolysis using electricity that itself has to be generated. A fuel cell is only as clean as its hydrogen supply.

**For the battery.** The charging infrastructure already exists, electricity is available everywhere, and a battery can be charged from renewable sources directly.

**Against the battery.** It takes **hours to charge**, it is **heavy**, it holds a **limited number of charge cycles** before it degrades, and it contains **scarce and toxic metals** that are difficult to dispose of.

**The decision.** For a car doing long distances with fast turnarounds, such as a lorry or a bus on a fixed route with its own refuelling point, the fuel cell wins. For a family car charged overnight at home, the battery wins, because the infrastructure exists and the hydrogen would probably have been made from fossil fuels anyway.

Notice what that last clause does: it makes the decision **conditional on something specific**, which is what turns a list into an evaluation.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- A **cell** contains **chemicals which react to produce electricity**.
- A **simple cell** is **two different metals in contact with an electrolyte**. Two pieces of the same metal give **zero** voltage.
- A **battery** is **two or more cells in series**, giving a **greater voltage**.
- The voltage depends on several factors, including the **type of electrode** and the **electrolyte**.
- The **greater the difference in reactivity** between the two metals, the **greater the voltage**.
- **Non-rechargeable**: the reactions **stop when one reactant is used up**. **Alkaline batteries are non-rechargeable.**
- **Rechargeable**: the reactions are **reversed when an external current is supplied**. Nothing new is added.
- A **fuel cell** is supplied by an **external source of fuel**, such as hydrogen, and **oxygen or air**. The fuel is **oxidised electrochemically to produce a potential difference**.
- In a hydrogen fuel cell the overall reaction is the **oxidation of hydrogen to produce water**: $2\text{H}_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
- **Higher tier**: at the negative electrode $2\text{H}_2 \rightarrow 4\text{H}^+ + 4e^-$; at the positive electrode $\text{O}_2 + 4\text{H}^+ + 4e^- \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. The alkaline forms are equally acceptable.
- To **evaluate**, give both sides and then **decide**, saying what the decision depends on. A fuel cell is only as clean as the hydrogen supplied to it.
- This topic is **chemistry only**.

questions.prompt: A student tests three cells, each with a copper electrode and one other metal, and records 2.7 V for magnesium, 1.1 V for zinc and 0.8 V for iron. Explain this pattern, and predict what would happen if both electrodes were copper.
questions.solution: In each of these cells the voltage produced depends on the two metals used as the electrodes. Magnesium is the most reactive of the three metals tested and iron is the least reactive of them, so magnesium is furthest from copper in the reactivity series, zinc is closer and iron is closer still. The greater the difference in reactivity between the two metals, the greater the voltage produced, which is exactly the order seen in the results: two point seven volts for magnesium, one point one for zinc and nought point eight for iron. If both electrodes were made of copper there would be no difference in reactivity between them at all, so no voltage would be produced and the reading would be zero.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The pattern.** The voltage depends on the two **electrodes**. Of the three metals tested, magnesium is the most reactive and iron the least, so **magnesium is furthest from copper** in the reactivity series, zinc is closer, and iron closer still.

The **greater the difference in reactivity, the greater the voltage** — which is the order in the results: 2.7 V, then 1.1 V, then 0.8 V.

**Two copper electrodes.** There would be **no difference in reactivity at all**, so no voltage: the reading would be **zero**. That is also why a simple cell needs two **different** metals.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the use of hydrogen fuel cells in cars in comparison with rechargeable batteries.
questions.solution: Hydrogen fuel cells have several advantages. At the point of use the only product is water, so no carbon dioxide or particulates are released where people are breathing. A fuel cell can be refuelled in minutes, whereas a rechargeable battery takes hours to charge, and a fuel cell loses capacity far more slowly than a battery degrades over hundreds of charges. For a given range the fuel cell system is also lighter, because the car carries fuel rather than a very heavy battery. There are, however, real disadvantages. Hydrogen is difficult to store, needing either very high pressure or very low temperature, and it is explosive, so it raises safety concerns. There are very few refuelling stations compared with the charging network that already exists for battery cars, and fuel cells rely on expensive catalysts. Most importantly, hydrogen has to be manufactured, usually from fossil fuels or by electrolysis using electricity that has itself been generated, so a fuel cell is only as clean as the hydrogen supplied to it. Rechargeable batteries can be charged directly from renewable electricity, although they contain scarce and toxic metals that are difficult to dispose of. On balance, fuel cells are the better choice for vehicles that travel long distances and need fast turnarounds, such as lorries or buses running from a depot with its own hydrogen supply. For an ordinary family car charged overnight at home, the rechargeable battery is the better choice, because the infrastructure already exists and the hydrogen would probably have been made from fossil fuels in any case.

**For the fuel cell.** At the point of use the only product is **water**, so no carbon dioxide or particulates where people breathe. It **refuels in minutes** rather than charging for hours, it **degrades far more slowly** than a battery, and for a given range the system is **lighter**.

**Against the fuel cell.** **Hydrogen is hard to store** — very high pressure or very low temperature — and it is **explosive**. There are **few refuelling stations**, and fuel cells need **expensive catalysts**. Above all, the hydrogen must be **made**, usually from fossil fuels or by electrolysis using generated electricity, so the cell is **only as clean as its supply**.

**The battery.** It charges from an **existing network**, and can take **renewable** electricity directly. Against it: **hours to charge**, **heavy**, a **limited number of cycles**, and **scarce and toxic metals** to dispose of.

**Decision.** For long distances with fast turnarounds — a lorry or a bus from a depot with its own hydrogen supply — the **fuel cell** wins. For a family car charged overnight, the **battery** wins: the infrastructure exists, and the hydrogen would likely have come from fossil fuels anyway.

The final mark is for making the decision **conditional on something specific**. That is what turns a list into an evaluation.

examTechnique.body:
Use the specification's own words for the definitions. A cell contains **chemicals which react to produce electricity**; a simple cell is **two different metals in contact with an electrolyte**; a battery is **two or more cells in series**.

When data is given, interpret it rather than reading it off: say that a bigger **difference in reactivity** gives a bigger voltage, and name which metals are furthest apart.

For recharging, say that an external current **reverses the reactions**. For a flat battery, say a **reactant has been used up**.

For a fuel cell, the fuel is **supplied from outside** and is **oxidised electrochemically** to produce a **potential difference**. In a hydrogen cell the only product is **water**.

At Higher tier, check a pair of half equations by adding them: the electrons must cancel and the result must be the overall equation. Balance atoms **and** charge in each half.

For an evaluation, argue both ways and then decide, naming the circumstances. Mentioning that the hydrogen has to be made is what separates the strongest answers.
examinerErrors: Saying a flat battery has run out of electricity, rather than that a reactant has been used up.
Saying recharging adds new chemicals, rather than reversing the reactions.
Using two electrodes of the same metal in a described cell, which would give zero voltage.
Reading a voltage table off without explaining it in terms of the difference in reactivity.
Saying a fuel cell is recharged. It is refuelled from an external supply.
Putting the electrons on the wrong side: oxidation loses them, so they go on the right.
Claiming a hydrogen fuel cell is emission free overall, ignoring how the hydrogen was made.
Listing advantages and disadvantages without reaching a decision.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer explains a voltage table rather than reporting it, naming the difference in reactivity as the cause and predicting zero for identical electrodes without being asked. It is precise that a flat cell has exhausted a reactant and that recharging reverses the reactions. At Higher tier it writes both half equations, balances charge as well as atoms, and demonstrates that they add to the overall equation with the electrons cancelling, treating that as the check rather than a flourish. In an evaluation it raises the manufacture of the hydrogen unprompted, since that is the point on which the environmental comparison actually turns, and it commits to a decision that names the circumstances in which it holds.
